paragraphs: The first and most important consequence of the principles established so far is this: only the general will can direct the State toward the purpose for which it was founded, _i.e._ the common good. If the clash of particular interests made it necessary to form societies, the agreement of those same interests made it possible. What these different interests have in common is what forms the social tie, and if there were no point on which they all agreed, no society could exist. It is on this common interest alone that every society ought to be governed.

I hold, then, that Sovereignty is nothing other than the exercise of the general will, and so it can never be given away. The Sovereign is nothing other than a collective being, and so it can be represented only by itself. Power may be transferred, but not will.

In fact, it is not impossible for a particular will to agree with the general will on some point, but it is impossible for that agreement to be lasting and constant. The particular will tends by its nature toward partiality, while the general will tends toward equality. It is even more impossible to have any guarantee of such agreement. Even if it always existed, it would be the result of chance, not of design. The Sovereign may well say, “At this moment I will what this man wills, or at least what he says he wills.” But it cannot say, “What he wills tomorrow, I will too.” For it is absurd for the will to bind itself for the future, and no will is obliged to consent to anything that is against the good of the being who wills. If the people, then, simply promises to obey, it dissolves itself by that very act and loses what makes it a people. The moment there is a master, there is no longer a Sovereign, and from that moment the body politic has ceased to exist.

None of this rules out that the commands of the rulers may pass for the general will, provided the Sovereign is free to object and does not. In that case, the silence of everyone is taken as the consent of the people. I will explain this later.
